A common weather pattern is the rain shadow effect, which occurs when air is pushed up a mountain and cools, causing moisture to condense and form clouds and rain. As the air continues to rise, it becomes drier on the other side of the mountain because it has already given up its moisture to form the clouds and rain. This creates a dry area on the leeward (downwind) side of the mountain range, known as a rain shadow.

For example, the Sierra Nevada mountain range in California creates a rain shadow, resulting in a dry area in the Central Valley. On the windward (upwind) side of the mountains, the air rises and cools, leading to a lot of rain and cloud formation. But on the leeward side, the air is drier and receives much less rainfall, creating a desert-like environment.

This pattern affects many mountain ranges around the world, like the Andes in South America, the Alps in Europe, and the Himalayas in Asia. The rain shadow effect can significantly impact local ecosystems, agriculture, and water resources in the affected areas.
